docs.title: robot_lab-sandbox
docs.text:
OS-level confinement for RobotLab skill scripts.

robot_lab core has no sandboxing and no execution limitations of its own — every AgentSkill script runs as a plain, unconfined OS process. robot_lab-sandbox plugs into core's one extension point for this (RobotLab::ScriptTool.executor) and, once turned on in config, confines each script to a declared, ceiling-clamped set of capabilities: which paths it may read and write, whether it may reach the network, and how long it may run.

require "robot_lab"
require "robot_lab/sandbox"
# RobotLab::ScriptTool.executor is now RobotLab::Sandbox::Executor.

# config/robot_lab.yml
sandbox:
  enabled: true
  fs_read: ["."]
  fs_write: ["./tmp"]
  network: false
  timeout: 60

On macOS, enabled: true wraps every skill script in a generated deny-by-default sandbox-exec (Seatbelt) profile. Elsewhere it's a passthrough with a one-time warning — confinement is currently macOS-only. Requiring the gem never changes behavior on its own; nothing is confined until sandbox.enabled is set.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Two things combine to decide what a skill script may actually do: what the skill declares it wants, and a global ceiling on what any skill may ever have. RobotLab::Capabilities (defined in robot_lab core, since AgentSkill needs it regardless of whether this gem is loaded) represents both sides and computes the intersection.

docs.title: The sandbox: Ceiling
docs.text:
Declared in robot_lab core's config/defaults.yml, read by Sandbox::Ceiling.build and Sandbox.enabled?:

sandbox:
  enabled: false        # opt-in; off = scripts run exactly as robot_lab core alone runs them
  fs_read: ["."]        # ceiling: paths any skill may read (relative to cwd)
  fs_write: []           # ceiling: paths any skill may write
  network: false          # ceiling: may any skill use the network
  timeout: 60               # ceiling: max seconds a skill script may run
Key Default Description sandbox.enabled false Turn on OS-level confinement for skill scripts. Read by RobotLab::Sandbox.enabled?. sandbox.fs_read ["."] Ceiling: paths any skill script may read (relative to cwd) sandbox.fs_write [] Ceiling: paths any skill script may write sandbox.network false Ceiling: whether any skill script may use the network sandbox.timeout 60 Ceiling: max seconds a skill script may run

Set these the same way as any other RobotLab config — a project's ./config/robot_lab.yml, the user's ~/.config/robot_lab/robot_lab.yml, or environment variables:

export ROBOT_LAB_SANDBOX__ENABLED=true
export ROBOT_LAB_SANDBOX__NETWORK=true
export ROBOT_LAB_SANDBOX__FS_WRITE=./tmp,./out

Environment variables arrive as strings, so this gem coerces every value it reads (Sandbox::Coerce) and takes the more restrictive reading when a value is unclear:

Key Accepted forms Anything else enabled on: true 1 yes on y t; off: false 0 no off n f, empty, unset (case-insensitive) confinement on network same words network denied fs_read / fs_write a YAML list, or a comma-separated string — timeout a positive whole number of seconds (30, "30") the default, 60

RobotLab::Sandbox::Ceiling.build returns the resulting ceiling. Core's own RobotLab::Capabilities.ceiling does not coerce — it reads ROBOT_LAB_SANDBOX__NETWORK=false as network allowed — so don't use it to inspect what this gem enforces.

This section exists in robot_lab core whether or not robot_lab-sandbox is loaded — core just doesn't act on it. Without this gem, scripts always run unconfined no matter what these values say.

docs.title: Per-Skill Declaration (SKILL.md Front Matter)
docs.text:
Each skill declares what it wants directly in its SKILL.md front matter, alongside name/description:

skills/deploy-checker/SKILL.md
---
name: deploy-checker
description: Verifies a deployment's health before promoting it.
fs_read: ["./data", "/etc/hosts"]
fs_write: ["./out"]
network: true
timeout: 30
trust: external   # or "core" for trusted, always-unconfined skills
---

AgentSkill parses this into a Capabilities object via Capabilities.from_front_matter — values are normalized and defaulted, so a malformed or partial declaration generally degrades to the safe default. One exception lives in core and is not fixable from this gem: a timeout that has no to_i (timeout: true, or a list) raises NoMethodError when the skill is loaded.

Key Type Default Coercion fs_read Array<String> [] Array(...) then to_s on each entry fs_write Array<String> [] Same network Boolean false Any truthy value becomes true timeout Integer 60 to_i; anything not positive becomes the default trust String "external" Must be "core" or "external", else falls back to "external"

docs.title: The Intersection
docs.text:
The script actually runs under the intersection of the skill's declared Capabilities and the sandbox: ceiling — computed by Sandbox::Grant.resolve, which applies core's Capabilities#intersect and then a symlink-resolved check on every path:

Field Rule fs_read / fs_write A requested path survives only when it is a ceiling root or lives beneath one. Both sides are File.expand_pathed first, so ~ and relative paths resolve before comparison. The path must then pass a second time with symlinks resolved on both sides (File.realpath): a path under the ceiling that is, or passes through, a symlink leading outside it is dropped, as is one that cannot be resolved (a symlink loop, a dangling symlink). network declared && ceiling — both sides must allow it. timeout The smaller of the two. trust The declared value, unchanged — the ceiling never carries a trust.

So a ceiling of fs_read: ["."] drops a skill's request for anything outside the working directory — a front-matter fs_read: ["~/.ssh"] grants nothing. (The ceiling only clamps what a skill adds: the Seatbelt profile's fixed system read paths — /usr, /bin, /sbin, /System, /Library, /opt, /private/etc, /dev, /var/select — and the skill's own directory are readable no matter what the ceiling says, see How It Works.) And a skill that doesn't declare network: true gets no network access no matter how permissive the ceiling is.

declared = RobotLab::Capabilities.from_front_matter(skill_front_matter)
grant    = RobotLab::Sandbox::Grant.resolve(declared, RobotLab::Sandbox::Ceiling.build)

docs.title: trust: core — Bypassing Confinement
docs.text: A skill declaring trust: core is exempt from OS-level confinement entirely — Sandbox.for always returns Sandbox::Null for it, on every platform, regardless of the sandbox: ceiling or sandbox.enabled. Reserve this for skill bundles you wrote and audited yourself; it is not something a skill should be able to grant itself casually, since it opts the script out of every confinement protection this gem provides (only the timeout bound still applies).

docs.title: What Changes When This Gem Isn't Loaded
docs.text: Nothing about Capabilities or the sandbox: config schema depends on robot_lab-sandbox — they live in core. What's missing without this gem is enforcement: RobotLab::ScriptTool.executor stays nil, so ScriptTool.execute always takes the plain Open3.capture2e path — no confinement, no timeout — regardless of what Capabilities or sandbox: say. See How It Works for the mechanics.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Ruby 4.0.9+ (per the gemspec's required_ruby_version)
  • robot_lab — robot_lab/sandbox requires RobotLab::ScriptTool to already be defined, so robot_lab must be required first.
  • macOS, if you want real OS-level confinement. On other platforms the gem still loads and wires itself in, but every script runs through Sandbox::Null (a passthrough) with a one-time warning logged.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Add to your Gemfile:

gem "robot_lab"
gem "robot_lab-sandbox"

Then:

bundle install

Or install directly:

gem install robot_lab-sandbox

docs.title: Enabling
docs.text:
Requiring the gem and turning on confinement are two separate steps — matching how robot_lab core's sandbox: config section already worked before this gem existed.

1. Require it, after robot_lab:

require "robot_lab"
require "robot_lab/sandbox"

This installs RobotLab::Sandbox::Executor as RobotLab::ScriptTool.executor and registers the gem via RobotLab.register_extension(:sandbox, ...). On its own this changes nothing yet — see How It Works for why: ScriptTool.execute only delegates to the executor when one is installed, and the executor itself checks Sandbox.enabled? before doing anything.

2. Turn on confinement in config:

# config/robot_lab.yml
sandbox:
  enabled: true
  fs_read: ["."]
  fs_write: []
  network: false
  timeout: 60

or via environment variables:

export ROBOT_LAB_SANDBOX__ENABLED=true

Environment variables arrive as strings; see Configuration for the accepted forms.

If robot_lab has not been loaded yet, require "robot_lab/sandbox" raises RobotLab::Sandbox::Error ("robot_lab must be loaded before robot_lab/sandbox").

docs.title: Minimal Example
docs.text:
require "robot_lab"
require "robot_lab/sandbox"

RobotLab.config.sandbox.enabled = true
RobotLab.config.sandbox.fs_write = ["./tmp"]

# A skill's SKILL.md declares what it wants; robot_lab core builds the
# Capabilities object from that front matter automatically when the skill
# is discovered. Here we build one directly to call ScriptTool ourselves:
capabilities = RobotLab::Capabilities.new(fs_write: ["./tmp"], timeout: 10)

tool = RobotLab::ScriptTool.from_path(
  "./skills/cleanup/scripts/purge_tmp.sh",
  capabilities: capabilities,
  skill_dir: "./skills/cleanup"
)

puts tool.call # runs confined on macOS, unconfined (with a warning) elsewhere

In practice you won't call ScriptTool.from_path directly — a discovered AgentSkill builds its own script_tools from its SKILL.md front matter and capabilities automatically. This example exists to show the pieces in isolation; see robot_lab's Skill Scripts and Sandboxing guide for the end-to-end skill-bundle path.

docs.title: Checking What's Installed
docs.text:
RobotLab.extension_loaded?(:sandbox)   # => true, once required
RobotLab::ScriptTool.executor          # => RobotLab::Sandbox::Executor, or nil
RobotLab::Sandbox.enabled?             # => reads config.sandbox.enabled
RobotLab::Sandbox::Ceiling.build       # => the coerced ceiling, as a Capabilities
RobotLab::Sandbox.macos?               # => RUBY_PLATFORM.include?("darwin")

docs.title: Key Constraints
docs.text:
• robot_lab must be required before robot_lab/sandbox — see Prerequisites above.
  • Confinement is opt-in via config.sandbox.enabled (default false). Requiring this gem does not turn confinement on by itself.
  • Real OS-level confinement is macOS-only. Off macOS, or for any skill declaring trust: core, every script runs through the Sandbox::Null passthrough regardless of sandbox.enabled.
  • The declared timeout: (per-skill or the config ceiling) only takes effect once this gem is loaded and sandbox.enabled is true — core alone, or this gem with sandboxing off, runs scripts with no timeout at all.

docs.title: The Extension Point: ScriptTool.executor
docs.text:
robot_lab core's RobotLab::ScriptTool exposes a single seam for confinement:

module RobotLab
  module ScriptTool
    class << self
      attr_accessor :executor
    end
  end
end

executor is nil by default. ScriptTool.execute(cmd, capabilities:, skill_dir:) checks it on every call:

def self.execute(cmd, capabilities:, skill_dir:)
  return executor.call(cmd, capabilities: capabilities, skill_dir: skill_dir) if executor

  output, status = Open3.capture2e(*cmd)
  format_result(output, status)
end

docs.title: ScriptTool.execute with no executor installed
docs.text: Without robot_lab-sandbox (or any other gem setting executor), every call takes the second branch: a plain Open3.capture2e, unconfined, with no timeout. This is exactly how core alone always behaved — the extension point was added specifically so this default stays true with zero code in core that knows anything about sandboxing.

docs.title: What loading this gem does
docs.text:
lib/robot_lab/sandbox.rb runs this at load time:

unless defined?(RobotLab::ScriptTool)
  raise RobotLab::Sandbox::Error, "robot_lab must be loaded before robot_lab/sandbox"
end

RobotLab::ScriptTool.executor = RobotLab::Sandbox::Executor

if RobotLab.respond_to?(:register_extension)
  RobotLab.register_extension(:sandbox, RobotLab::Sandbox)
end

From that point on, every ScriptTool.execute call delegates entirely to RobotLab::Sandbox::Executor.call. Core no longer knows or cares what the executor does with capabilities or how — or whether — it bounds execution time; that's this gem's job from here down.

docs.title: Sandbox::Executor — What Actually Runs
docs.text:
module_function

def call(cmd, capabilities:, skill_dir:)
  unless Sandbox.enabled?
    output, status = Open3.capture2e(*cmd)
    return RobotLab::ScriptTool.format_result(output, status)
  end

  grant   = Grant.resolve(capabilities, Ceiling.build)
  sandbox = Sandbox.for(grant, skill_dir: skill_dir)
  begin
    output, status = run_with_timeout(sandbox.wrap(cmd), grant.timeout)
    format_result(output, status)
  ensure
    sandbox.cleanup
  end
end

Two paths, gated by Sandbox.enabled? (which reads config.sandbox.enabled, default false, accepting the string forms an environment variable delivers — see Configuration):

  1. Disabled — identical to core's own unconfined path. Loading this gem with sandbox.enabled: false changes nothing observable.
  2. Enabled — computes the effective grant (skill's declared Capabilities ∩ the config ceiling, see Configuration), picks a strategy via Sandbox.for, wraps the command, runs it under a timeout, and always calls sandbox.cleanup in an ensure — even if the run raised or timed out. Executor.format_result is core's ScriptTool.format_result plus one case: a process that died from a signal is reported as "Error (killed by signal N):\n<output>".

docs.title: Strategy Selection: Sandbox.for
docs.text:
module_function

def for(grant, skill_dir:, macos: macos?)
  return Null.new if grant.core?
  return Seatbelt.new(grant, skill_dir: skill_dir) if macos

  warn_once_non_macos
  Null.new
end

Selection order:

  1. trust: core (grant.core?) → always Sandbox::Null, on every platform.
  2. macOS → Sandbox::Seatbelt.
  3. Anything else → Sandbox::Null, plus a one-time warn-level log message (Sandbox.warn_once_non_macos, idempotent — a run with many scripts doesn't flood the log).

macos: is injectable (defaults to the real RUBY_PLATFORM check) so both branches are testable on any host without stubbing.

docs.title: Sandbox::Null — the Passthrough
docs.text:
class Null
  def wrap(cmd) = cmd
  def cleanup; end
end

wrap is the identity function; cleanup is a no-op. Used off-macOS and for trust: core skills — the command runs exactly as it would with no executor installed at all, except still bounded by Executor's timeout.

docs.title: Sandbox::Seatbelt — Real Confinement on macOS
docs.text:
wrap(cmd) generates a Seatbelt profile to a Tempfile and returns:

["sandbox-exec", "-f", profile_path, *cmd]

docs.title: The generated profile
docs.text:
(version 1)
(import "bsd.sb")
(deny default)
(allow process-fork)
(allow process-exec)
(allow sysctl-read)
(allow mach-lookup)
(allow file-read-metadata)
(allow file-read* (subpath "/usr") (subpath "/bin") ... (subpath <skill_dir>) (subpath <granted fs_read>) ...)
(allow file-write* (literal "/dev/null") ... (subpath <granted fs_write>))
(allow network*)   ; only present when the grant allows network

Built from three pieces:

Piece Source Deny by default (deny default) — nothing is allowed unless an explicit (allow ...) clause says so. Boot allowances (import "bsd.sb") (the base rules a process needs to start — dyld, mach bootstrap, etc.; without it a deny-default profile aborts the binary before it runs), plus process-fork, process-exec, sysctl-read, mach-lookup, and file-read-metadata on any path (so the interpreter can stat/traverse to reach granted files — reading file contents stays restricted separately). The grant file-read* on Seatbelt::SYSTEM_READ (/usr /bin /sbin /System /Library /opt /private/etc /dev /var/select) plus the skill directory plus the grant's fs_read; file-write* on Seatbelt::DEV_WRITE (/dev/null /dev/stdout /dev/stderr /dev/dtracehelper /dev/tty) plus the grant's fs_write; network* only when grant.network is true.

$HOME is never in any of these lists — it is never implicitly readable. The exceptions are the skill directory itself (always granted, even when it lives under $HOME), file metadata (file-read-metadata is allowed on every path, so a confined script can stat any file but not read or list it), and whatever bsd.sb itself allows (e.g. .CFUserTextEncoding). See Troubleshooting for the direct consequence of that.

docs.title: Path canonicalization
docs.text:
Every path is resolved to its symlink-free real path before being written into the profile:

def canonicalize(paths)
  Array(paths).filter_map { |p| Paths.real(p) }.uniq
end

This matters because macOS symlinks /tmp → /private/tmp, /var → /private/var, etc. — the kernel matches Seatbelt rules against the real path, so a rule written against the logical /tmp/... path would silently never match. For a write target that doesn't exist yet, Paths.real walks up to the nearest existing ancestor, resolves that, and re-appends the non-existent remainder. A path that cannot be resolved (a symlink loop, a dangling symlink) yields nil and is left out of the profile.

The same resolution guards the grant itself: Grant.resolve only keeps a declared path whose real location is inside a real ceiling root, so a symlink under the ceiling that points elsewhere is dropped before a profile is ever generated (see Configuration).

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text: wrap writes the profile via Tempfile.create; cleanup unlinks it and swallows any error (an already-removed file is fine). Executor.call always calls sandbox.cleanup in an ensure, so a profile file is never leaked even when the script raises or times out.

docs.title: Timeout Enforcement
docs.text:
Executor.run_with_timeout(cmd, timeout) runs the (possibly Seatbelt-wrapped) command in its own process group and bounds the whole execution — the process itself, not just its output — at timeout seconds:

module_function

def run_with_timeout(cmd, timeout)
  limit = Coerce.duration(timeout)
  Open3.popen2e(child_env, *cmd, pgroup: true) do |stdin, out, wait|
    stdin.close
    supervise(out, wait, limit)
  end
end

def supervise(out, wait, limit)
  buffer = +""
  reader = Thread.new { drain(out, buffer) }
  return [text(buffer), wait.value] if finished_within?(limit, wait, reader)

  terminate(wait.pid)
  reader.join(POLL)
  reader.kill
  ["#{text(buffer)}\n[killed: exceeded #{limit}s]", nil]
end

A reader thread drains combined stdout+stderr into a buffer while finished_within? waits on the process. The run counts as finished only when the process has exited and its output has reached EOF inside the limit, so neither a script that closes its output and keeps running nor a background child left holding the pipe escapes the bound.

On expiry, terminate sends SIGTERM to the whole process group (Process.kill("TERM", -pid) — pgroup: true makes the child its own group leader), so a script that spawned children takes them down with it. Anything still alive after Executor::KILL_GRACE (2 seconds) gets SIGKILL. terminate never raises — a group that is already gone is not an error — and refuses a pid of 1 or less. A process that leaves the group (setsid) is not reached by the kill; it remains inside the Seatbelt profile.

A nil status return value is ScriptTool.format_result's signal for "Error (timed out):\n<output>", which is what the LLM sees; a nil status is never confused with a real (even nonzero) exit code. <output> is whatever the script printed before the kill, followed by "\n[killed: exceeded <timeout>s]".

Coerce.duration keeps any positive, finite number and replaces anything else (nil, true, a list, a non-numeric string, zero or a negative) with the 60-second default, so a malformed timeout cannot crash the executor. child_env passes the real working directory as PWD: without it the shell calls getcwd(), which fails under Seatbelt because the working directory's ancestors are not readable, and prints a shell-init: error retrieving current directory line into the output. It grants no access.

The timeout used is grant.timeout — the smaller of the skill's declared timeout: and the config ceiling's sandbox.timeout (see Configuration). This bound applies only when this gem is loaded and sandboxing is enabled; core alone (or this gem with sandbox.enabled: false) never times a script out.

docs.title: Extension Registration
docs.text:
RobotLab.register_extension(:sandbox, RobotLab::Sandbox) lets other code detect this gem is loaded without depending on it directly:

RobotLab.extension_loaded?(:sandbox)  # => true, once required
RobotLab.extension(:sandbox)          # => RobotLab::Sandbox, or nil

This follows the same pattern every other RobotLab extension gem (robot_lab-audit, robot_lab-durable, etc.) uses — register_extension is a no-op-safe check (RobotLab.respond_to?(:register_extension)), so robot_lab/sandbox never raises on this line even against an unusually old robot_lab core.

docs.title: Interpreter installed under $HOME is invisible
docs.text:
Symptom: a script fails as soon as it invokes its interpreter, with something like ruby: Operation not permitted (exit 126, e.g. an rbenv shim) or Killed: 9 (exit 137, a compiled binary), but the same script runs fine with sandbox.enabled: false.

Cause: the generated Seatbelt profile never grants read access to $HOME, on purpose — that's what keeps SSH keys and cloud credentials out of reach of a confined script. But it also means any interpreter installed under $HOME (rbenv, asdf, mise, a Homebrew prefix under ~, ~/.gem, a project-local bundle path under ~/.bundle) is unreadable to the sandboxed process. The skill script itself still starts — ScriptTool always runs it as bash <script>, ignoring its shebang — but the first command that lives under $HOME cannot be loaded.

Fix: either

  • Grant the interpreter's install path explicitly in the skill's fs_read: 
    fs_read: ["~/.rbenv"]
    (this still goes through the config sandbox.fs_read ceiling — the ceiling must permit it too, see Configuration), or
  • Mark the skill trust: core if you wrote and audited it yourself — this bypasses confinement entirely, see Configuration — trust: core.

docs.title: A path I granted is still denied
docs.text:
Symptom: a script writes to (or reads from) a path you declared in fs_write/fs_read, but the write or read fails with Operation not permitted (or comes back empty if the script discards errors), even though sandbox.enabled: true and the skill's front matter looks right.

Checklist:

  1. Is the path inside the config ceiling? The effective grant is the intersection of what the skill declares and config.sandbox.fs_read/ fs_write — a path outside every ceiling root is dropped silently, even if the skill asks for it. Check RobotLab::Sandbox::Ceiling.build.fs_read / .fs_write in a console.
  2. Is it a symlinked path? macOS symlinks /tmp → /private/tmp, /var → /private/var. The profile is generated against the resolved real path — if you're comparing against the logical path elsewhere (e.g. in a test assertion), resolve it with File.realpath first. See How It Works — Path canonicalization.
  3. Does the path leave the ceiling through a symlink? A granted path is kept only when its real location is inside a real ceiling root. A symlink under the working directory that points somewhere else is dropped, and so is a symlink loop or a dangling symlink. Grant the real target, and make sure the ceiling covers it.
  4. Does the path exist yet, for a write target? Canonicalization walks up to the nearest existing ancestor to resolve symlinks, then re-appends the rest — if an intermediate directory is later created as a symlink, the kernel resolves it and the write lands outside the granted path, so it is denied. Prefer granting an existing parent directory over a not-yet-created nested path.
  5. Is trust: core set? A core skill bypasses the sandbox entirely — if you're debugging a denial and the skill is trust: core, the sandbox isn't involved at all; look elsewhere (permissions, the script itself).

You can inspect the exact profile a skill's declaration produces without running anything:

declared = RobotLab::Capabilities.new(fs_read: ["./data"], fs_write: ["./out"])
grant    = RobotLab::Sandbox::Grant.resolve(declared, RobotLab::Sandbox::Ceiling.build)
puts RobotLab::Sandbox::Seatbelt.new(grant, skill_dir: "./skills/example").profile_text

docs.title: Nothing is confined, even with sandbox.enabled: true
docs.text:
Symptom: scripts still behave as if sandboxing were off — no denials, no warnings, everything just works as before.

Checklist:

  1. Is RobotLab::Sandbox.enabled? actually true? Check it in a console rather than trusting the config file — it is the exact test the executor uses. true/1/yes/on (as a boolean or an env-var string) turn it on; false/0/no/off, empty, or unset leave it off.
  2. Is robot_lab/sandbox actually required? require "robot_lab/sandbox" must run after require "robot_lab". Check: 
    RobotLab::ScriptTool.executor  # nil means this gem was never loaded
  3. Is the skill trust: core? Always bypasses confinement — see above.
  4. Are you off macOS? Confinement is macOS-only; elsewhere every script runs through Sandbox::Null (a passthrough) with a one-time warning logged (Sandbox: OS-level confinement is only available on macOS; ...). Check RobotLab::Sandbox.macos?.

docs.title: A script that used to finish now gets killed with [killed: exceeded Ns]
docs.text:
Cause: once this gem is loaded and sandboxing is enabled, every script run is bounded by the effective grant's timeout — the smaller of the skill's declared timeout: and config.sandbox.timeout (default 60). Core alone never enforced a timeout at all, so a slow script that worked fine before can now hit this for the first time.

The bound covers the whole run, not just its output: on expiry the script's process group gets SIGTERM, then SIGKILL two seconds later if anything is still alive. What the script printed before the kill is returned ahead of the [killed: exceeded Ns] marker. A process that leaves the group (setsid) is not reached by the kill, though it stays inside the Seatbelt profile.

Fix: raise the skill's declared timeout: in its SKILL.md front matter, and/or raise the config ceiling's sandbox.timeout — whichever is currently the smaller (and therefore binding) value.

docs.title: robot_lab/sandbox raises on require
docs.text:
RobotLab::Sandbox::Error: robot_lab must be loaded before robot_lab/sandbox

Cause: require "robot_lab/sandbox" ran before require "robot_lab" (or robot_lab failed to load for some other reason first). robot_lab/sandbox checks defined?(RobotLab::ScriptTool) at load time and raises immediately rather than silently no-op-ing, since a sandbox gem that failed to install itself and said nothing would be far more dangerous than one that's loud about it.

Fix: reorder your requires (or Gemfile-driven autoload order) so robot_lab loads first.
